items.followUp: Describe single, double and triple covalent bonds, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Identifies what is shared in a single covalent bond.
rubric.description: Single bond: one pair of electrons is shared.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that one pair of electrons is shared in a single bond.

rubric.why: Gives a correct example of a molecule with a single covalent bond.
rubric.description: Example of a single bond: H₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct single-bond example.

rubric.why: Identifies what is shared in a double covalent bond.
rubric.description: Double bond: two pairs of electrons are shared.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that two pairs of electrons are shared in a double bond.

rubric.why: Gives a correct example of a molecule with a double covalent bond.
rubric.description: Example of a double bond: O₂; triple bond: three pairs of electrons are shared, as in N₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example of either a double or triple bond, with its corresponding shared-pair description.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms share pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond is formed by sharing one pair of electrons; for example, H₂.
A double covalent bond is formed by sharing two pairs of electrons; for example, O₂.
A triple covalent bond is formed by sharing three pairs of electrons; for example, N₂.

items.followUp: Describe how to prepare a dilute solution from a concentrated solution, including the dilution formula.

rubric.why: Uses the dilution relationship to determine the required volume of concentrated solution.
rubric.description: State the dilution formula, M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula.

rubric.why: Shows that the amount of concentrated solution needed is determined before dilution.
rubric.description: Calculate the required volume of concentrated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the required volume is calculated from the formula.

rubric.why: Identifies suitable equipment for making a solution up to a precise final volume.
rubric.description: Place some distilled water in a volumetric flask.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a volumetric flask as the vessel used.

rubric.why: Shows that the calculated volume is measured and transferred accurately.
rubric.description: Measure the calculated volume of concentrated solution with a pipette and transfer it to the flask.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for measuring and transferring the required concentrated solution.

rubric.why: Completes the dilution to the required volume and ensures the solution is mixed.
rubric.description: Add distilled water up to the calibration mark and mix thoroughly. For concentrated acids, add acid to water slowly, never water to acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for making up to the mark and mixing; accept the acid-safety instruction as supporting detail.

modelAnswer: Use the dilution formula M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ to calculate the volume of concentrated solution required.
Put some distilled water into a volumetric flask.
Measure the calculated volume of concentrated solution with a pipette and transfer it to the flask.
Add distilled water until the bottom of the meniscus reaches the calibration mark.
Stopper the flask and mix the solution thoroughly. When diluting an acid, add the acid slowly to water, never water to acid.

rubric.why: Identifies the subject as the study of chemical processes in the environment.
rubric.description: Environmental chemistry studies chemical processes in the environment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying chemical processes occurring in the environment.

rubric.why: Recognizes the effects of chemicals or human activity on the environment.
rubric.description: It also considers the effects of pollutants and human activities on the environment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning environmental effects, pollutants, or human activities.

modelAnswer: Environmental chemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies chemical processes occurring in the environment and the effects of pollutants and human activities on it.

rubric.why: Specifies that gram molecular mass refers to a mole of molecules.
rubric.description: It is the mass of one mole of a substance’s molecules, expressed in grams.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating gram molecular mass to one mole of molecules.

rubric.why: States the relationship between gram molecular mass and molecular mass.
rubric.description: Its numerical value is equal to the molecular mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its numerical value equals the molecular mass.

modelAnswer: Gram molecular mass is the mass, in grams, of one mole of a substance’s molecules.
Its numerical value is equal to the molecular mass of the substance.

items.followUp: Name two radioisotopes used in medicine and state one use of each.

rubric.why: Names a radioisotope used to treat cancer.
rubric.description: Cobalt-60 is used in cancer treatment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming cobalt-60.

rubric.why: Names another radioisotope used in cancer treatment.
rubric.description: Radium-226 is another accepted example; iodine-131 is also used in certain cancer treatments.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a second valid radioisotope used in cancer treatment.

modelAnswer: Cobalt-60 is used in the treatment of cancer.
Radium-226 is another radioisotope used in the treatment of cancer.

items.followUp: State the modern periodic law and identify the quantity on which it is based.

rubric.why: Gives the defining relationship between elemental properties and atomic number.
rubric.description: The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the complete statement; award 1 mark if only the periodic nature or atomic number dependence is stated.

modelAnswer: The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.

items.followUp: Explain why atomic size generally increases down a group.

rubric.why: States the direction of the electronegativity trend down a group.
rubric.description: Electronegativity decreases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electronegativity decreases down a group.

rubric.why: Explains that increased atomic size and shielding weaken the nucleus's attraction for bonding electrons.
rubric.description: Down a group, atomic size and shielding increase, so the nucleus attracts shared electrons less strongly.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid explanation involving increased distance, atomic size, or shielding and weaker nuclear attraction.

modelAnswer: The number of electron shells and shielding increase, so the shared electrons are farther from the nucleus and experience less nuclear attraction.

items.followUp: Why is the density of ice lower than that of liquid water?

rubric.why: States the property that explains why ice floats.
rubric.description: Ice is less dense than liquid water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ice has a lower density than water.

rubric.why: Explains the lower density using the structure of ice.
rubric.description: Hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open structure in ice, making them farther apart; the same mass occupies more volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that ice’s open structure increases its volume and lowers its density.

modelAnswer: Ice floats on water because it is less dense than liquid water.
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open structure in ice, so the molecules are farther apart and the same mass occupies more volume.
